claim: Electrophysiological recordings were performed in the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) of rats as they explored a squared open field arena and foraged for scattered chocolate pellets.
source: We performed electrophysiological recordings of neuronal activity in RSC (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) of rats as they explored a squared open field arena and foraged for scattered chocolate pellets (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript directly describes the experimental procedure performed.

claim: A total of 5415 RSC neurons were recorded across eight animals in 82 sessions.
source: We recorded the activity of 5415 RSC neurons across eight animals (n = 82 sessions) and observed a subpopulation of cells that fired consistently at the edge of the arena (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers from the experimental data collection.

claim: A subpopulation of RSC cells fired consistently at the edge of the arena.
source: We recorded the activity of 5415 RSC neurons across eight animals (n = 82 sessions) and observed a subpopulation of cells that fired consistently at the edge of the arena (Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes an observed firing pattern in the recorded neurons.

claim: RSC border cells exhibited a variety of preferred firing distances from the wall, ranging from very near proximity up to 15-18 cm away.
source: Across this subgroup, there was a variety of preferred firing distances from the wall, ranging from very near proximity up to a body-length (15–18 cm) away.
evidence: The manuscript describes the range of firing distances observed in the data.

claim: RSC border cells fire throughout the environment on each of the four available walls, unlike traditional border cells found in MEC and subiculum.
source: Unlike traditional border cells found in MEC and subiculum (Solstad et al., 2008; Stewart et al., 2014), these border responses occurred throughout the environment on each of the four available walls.
evidence: The manuscript compares the observed RSC border cells to previously reported border cells in other brain regions.

claim: RSC border cells form multiple firing fields that are not necessarily directly connected to the wall.
source: RSC border cells furthermore form multiple firing fields that are not necessarily directly connected to the wall.
evidence: The manuscript describes a characteristic of the observed firing patterns.

claim: The original border score identified only a small fraction of border cells in RSC because it is based on the occupancy of a single firing field along a wall and is strongly biased to connected bins.
source: Typical border cell classification using the original border score (Solstad et al., 2008) identified only a small fraction of border cells in RSC, as this score is based on the occupancy of a single firing field along a wall and is strongly biased to connected bins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The manuscript explains why the traditional classification method was inadequate for RSC border cells, referencing both the original method and supplementary figure data.

claim: A new model-based approach using a template-matching procedure was developed to classify border cells in RSC.
source: We thus developed a new model-based approach using a template-matching procedure to classify these border cells in RSC (Figure 1D–F), based on Grossberger et al., 2018.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development of a new classification method.

claim: The Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) is a normalized score calculated as the minimum cost required to match a cell's firing rate map with the template distribution by moving firing rate units.
source: The EMD is a normalized score, calculated as the minimum cost required to match a cell's firing rate map with the template distribution by moving firing rate units, also known as the Wasserstein distance.
evidence: The manuscript defines the EMD metric used in the analysis.

claim: The EMD metric is sensitive to changes in the geometric shape of rate maps but robust to small variations of preferred firing distances or pixel-by-pixel jittering.
source: While this metric is sensitive to a change in the geometric shape of rate maps, it is robust to small variations of preferred firing distances or pixel-by-pixel jittering, giving a single metric that can quantitatively assess changes in the cell's spatial tuning as a function of experimental manipulations, such as reshaping of the maze or adding an object or wall.
evidence: The manuscript describes the properties of the EMD metric.

claim: Border cells were defined as cells with an EMD score below the 1st percentile of a spike-shuffled null distribution of 0.191 and an average firing rate above 0.5 Hz.
source: Border cells were defined as cells with a low dissimilarity EMD score below the 1st percentile of a spike-shuffled null distribution of 0.191, and an average firing rate (FR) above 0.5 Hz.
evidence: The manuscript provides the specific criteria used for border cell classification.

claim: 485 out of 5415 RSC cells (9.0%) passed the border cell classification criteria.
source: In total, 485 out of 5415 RSC cells (9.0%) passed this criterion (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2G), where neurons showed no relationship between their overall spiking rate and associated EMD score (Pearson's correlation: r = 0.037, p=0.42; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of cells classified as border cells.

claim: There was no relationship between neurons' overall spiking rate and associated EMD score (Pearson's correlation: r = 0.037, p=0.42).
source: In total, 485 out of 5415 RSC cells (9.0%) passed this criterion (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2G), where neurons showed no relationship between their overall spiking rate and associated EMD score (Pearson's correlation: r = 0.037, p=0.42; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical test result showing no correlation.

claim: Selected border cells had a similar distribution of average firing rates compared to other recorded cells (border cells: FR = 2.97 ± 0.20 Hz, others: FR = 3.25 ± 0.07 Hz; Wilcoxon ranksum test: z = 0.057, p=0.955).
source: Selected border cells had a similar distribution of average firing rates compared to other recorded cells (border cells: FR = 2.97 ± 0.20 Hz, others: FR = 3.25 ± 0.07 Hz; Wilcoxon ranksum test: z = 0.057, p=0.955; Figure 1G), but had significantly higher spatial correlations between the first and last recording sessions (border cells: r = 0.52 ± 0.008, others: r = 0.20 ± 0.003; Wilcoxon ranksum test: z = −24.50, p=1.60 × 10−132; Figure 1H).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of firing rates between border cells and other cells.

claim: Border cells had significantly higher spatial correlations between the first and last recording sessions compared to other cells (border cells: r = 0.52 ± 0.008, others: r = 0.20 ± 0.003; Wilcoxon ranksum test: z = −24.50, p=1.60 × 10−132).
source: Selected border cells had a similar distribution of average firing rates compared to other recorded cells (border cells: FR = 2.97 ± 0.20 Hz, others: FR = 3.25 ± 0.07 Hz; Wilcoxon ranksum test: z = 0.057, p=0.955; Figure 1G), but had significantly higher spatial correlations between the first and last recording sessions (border cells: r = 0.52 ± 0.008, others: r = 0.20 ± 0.003; Wilcoxon ranksum test: z = −24.50, p=1.60 × 10−132; Figure 1H).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of spatial correlations between border cells and other cells.

claim: Border cells were recorded across the granular and dysgranular regions of the RSC.
source: Border cells were recorded across the granular and dysgranular regions of the RSC, and had waveform properties similar to other cells recorded on the same tetrodes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B,D,E).
evidence: The manuscript describes the anatomical locations where border cells were found.

claim: Border cells had waveform properties similar to other cells recorded on the same tetrodes.
source: Border cells were recorded across the granular and dysgranular regions of the RSC, and had waveform properties similar to other cells recorded on the same tetrodes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B,D,E).
evidence: The manuscript reports a comparison of electrophysiological properties.

claim: Border cells showed activity already from the beginning of the session and did not need time for adaptation in a novel arena and experimental room.
source: Border cells showed activity already from the beginning of the session and did not need time for adaptation in a novel arena and experimental room (first-half familiar session, FR = 1.98 ± 0.42 Hz; first-half novel session, FR = 2.30 ± 0.53 Hz, p=0.56; second half novel session, FR = 1.71 ± 0.54 Hz, p=0.68; Wilcoxon signed-rank test; n = 14 border cells; Figure 1—figure supplement 4D–G).
evidence: The manuscript reports data from novel environment experiments showing immediate border cell activity.

claim: Firing of RSC border cells was modulated by the running speed of the animal, with lower firing rates in the low-speed range (p<0.05 in the range of 0–12 cm/s).
source: While firing of RSC border cells was additionally modulated by the running speed of the animal, with lower firing rates in the low-speed range (p<0.05 in the range of 0–12 cm/s; Wilcoxon ranksum test; Figure 1—figure supplement 3G), this modulation could not account for the cell's spatial tuning, as the animal's average speed was uniform across space and unrelated to the distance to any boundary (non-significant in the range of 5–45 cm; Wilcoxon ranksum test against overall median; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.005; Figure 1—figure supplement 3F,H).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of speed modulation of border cell firing.

claim: Speed modulation could not account for the cell's spatial tuning because the animal's average speed was uniform across space and unrelated to the distance to any boundary.
source: While firing of RSC border cells was additionally modulated by the running speed of the animal, with lower firing rates in the low-speed range (p<0.05 in the range of 0–12 cm/s; Wilcoxon ranksum test; Figure 1—figure supplement 3G), this modulation could not account for the cell's spatial tuning, as the animal's average speed was uniform across space and unrelated to the distance to any boundary (non-significant in the range of 5–45 cm; Wilcoxon ranksum test against overall median; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.005; Figure 1—figure supplement 3F,H).
evidence: The manuscript provides statistical evidence that speed does not explain spatial tuning.

claim: Running speed and wall-distance are two independent factors that explain the activity of RSC cells.
source: Applying an unbiased classification approach based on linear-nonlinear models (Hardcastle et al., 2017) showed that running speed and wall-distance are two independent factors that explain the activity of RSC cells, confirming that RSC border and speed tuning are separately expressed features (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from a linear-nonlinear model analysis.

claim: Border cells formed new firing fields around added walls, with firing rate inside a region-of-interest around the wall increasing significantly in the added wall sessions (Regular: FR = 1.19 ± 0.13 Hz; Added wall: FR = 1.58 ± 0.21 Hz; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = −2.67, p=0.0076; n = 42 border cells).
source: Border cells formed new firing fields around the added walls accordingly, as their firing rate inside a region-of-interest (ROI; 15 × 5 spatial bins) around the wall increased significantly in the added wall sessions (Regular: FR = 1.19 ± 0.13 Hz; Added wall: FR = 1.58 ± 0.21 Hz; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = −2.67, p=0.0076; n = 42 border cells; Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of firing rate changes when walls were added.

claim: Spatial correlations between rate maps dropped sharply when comparing regular versus added wall sessions (Reg-Reg: r = 0.51 ± 0.04, Reg-Wall: r = 0.25 ± 0.04; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 4.43, p=9.31 × 10−6).
source: This was accompanied by a sharp drop in spatial correlations between rate maps of regular versus added wall sessions (Reg-Reg: r = 0.51 ± 0.04, Reg-Wall: r = 0.25 ± 0.04; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 4.43, p=9.31 × 10−6; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.025; Figure 2D), while correlations remained high when comparing within session types (Wall-Wall: r = 0.47 ± 0.03; Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Reg-Reg correlation: z = 0.63, p=0.53; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.025; Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of spatial correlations across different session types.

claim: Correlations remained high when comparing within session types (Wall-Wall: r = 0.47 ± 0.03; Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Reg-Reg correlation: z = 0.63, p=0.53).
source: This was accompanied by a sharp drop in spatial correlations between rate maps of regular versus added wall sessions (Reg-Reg: r = 0.51 ± 0.04, Reg-Wall: r = 0.25 ± 0.04; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 4.43, p=9.31 × 10−6; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.025; Figure 2D), while correlations remained high when comparing within session types (Wall-Wall: r = 0.47 ± 0.03; Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Reg-Reg correlation: z = 0.63, p=0.53; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.025; Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing stable correlations within session types.

claim: The EMD metric showed a significant increase in dissimilarity between rate maps of added wall sessions and the original boundary template.
source: The EMD metric furthermore showed a significant increase in dissimilarity between rate maps of these added wall sessions and the original boundary template (Normalized boundary EMD score: R1, 1.0 ± 0, W1, 1.178 ± 0.03, W2, 1.223 ± 0.03, R2, 1.016 ± 0.01; Friedman test: X2(3)=77.9, p=8.6 × 10−17; Post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank test: R1-W1, z = −5.35, p=9.0 × 10−8, R1-W2, z = −5.58, p=2.37 × 10−8, R1-R2, z = −1.27, p=0.20; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.017; Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of EMD scores with the boundary template.

claim: The dissimilarity between rate maps and an 'added wall' template decreased significantly in added wall sessions.
source: In contrast, the dissimilarity between the same rate maps and an 'added wall' template decreased significantly (Normalized wall EMD score: R1, 1.0 ± 0, W1, 0.918 ± 0.02, W2, 0.934 ± 0.03, R2, 1.057 ± 0.02; Friedman test: X2(3)=33.7, p=2.3 × 10−7; Post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank test: R1-W1, z = −3.89, p=9.8 × 10−5, R1-W2, z = 2.59, p=0.0095, R1-R2, z = −2.22, p=0.027; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.017; Figure 2E), indicating that firing fields of border cells incorporated boundary information of the added wall.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of EMD scores with the added wall template.

claim: Firing fields of border cells incorporated boundary information of the added wall.
source: In contrast, the dissimilarity between the same rate maps and an 'added wall' template decreased significantly (Normalized wall EMD score: R1, 1.0 ± 0, W1, 0.918 ± 0.02, W2, 0.934 ± 0.03, R2, 1.057 ± 0.02; Friedman test: X2(3)=33.7, p=2.3 × 10−7; Post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank test: R1-W1, z = −3.89, p=9.8 × 10−5, R1-W2, z = 2.59, p=0.0095, R1-R2, z = −2.22, p=0.027; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.017; Figure 2E), indicating that firing fields of border cells incorporated boundary information of the added wall.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the EMD analysis results.

claim: RSC border cells maintained tuning only to the outer walls and did not fire when objects were inside their receptive field (Regular: FR = 1.39 ± 0.26 Hz; Added object: FR = 1.42 ± 0.21 Hz; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = −0.63, p=0.53; n = 23 border cells).
source: Contrary to an added wall, RSC border cells maintained tuning only to the outer walls and did not fire whenever objects were inside their receptive field (Circular ROI, eight bins in diameter; Regular: FR = 1.39 ± 0.26 Hz; Added object: FR = 1.42 ± 0.21 Hz; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = −0.63, p=0.53; n = 23 border cells; Figure 2H).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing no change in firing rate near objects.

claim: EMD analyses showed a significant increase in dissimilarity to the boundary template in the object sessions.
source: EMD analyses however showed a significant increase in dissimilarity to the boundary template in the object sessions (Normalized boundary EMD score: R1, 1.0 ± 0, O1, 1.097 ± 0.031, O2, 1.079 ± 0.028, R2, 1.024 ± 0.021; Friedman test: X2(3)=14.7, p=0.002; Post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank test: R1-O1, z = −2.74, p=0.006, R1-O2, z = −2.62, p=0.009, R1-R2, z = −1.00, p=0.32; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.017; Figure 2J), indicating changes in the rate maps by the object.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of EMD scores in object sessions.

claim: Fitting an 'object' template did not lead to a decrease in dissimilarity during object sessions, indicating cells did not form new firing fields around the object.
source: This change was not due to new firing fields around the object, however, because fitting an 'object' template did not lead to a decrease in dissimilarity during object sessions (Normalized object EMD score: R1, 1.0 ± 0, O1, 1.026 ± 0.026, O2, 0.995 ± 0.029, R2, 0.990 ± 0.025; Friedman test: X2(3)=2.32, p=0.51; Figure 2J).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing no fit to object template.

claim: Spatial correlations did not drop when comparing rate maps between regular and object sessions for either the outer rows of pixels adjacent to the walls or the inner area surrounding the object.
source: The maintenance of original firing fields was further confirmed by spatial correlations across session types that did not drop when comparing rate maps between regular and object sessions, neither for the outer rows of pixels adjacent to the walls (Reg-Reg: r = 0.36 ± 0.07, Object-Object: r = 0.47 ± 0.07; z = −0.88, p=0.38; Reg-Object: r = 0.45 ± 0.07; comparing with R-R: z = −1.28, p=0.20; comparing with R-O: z = 1.16, p=0.25; Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.017; Figure 2I, right panel), nor the inner area surrounding the object (Reg-Reg: r = 0.29 ± 0.07, Object-Object: r = 0.49 ± 0.05: z = −1.58, p=0.11; Reg-Object: r = 0.33 ± 0.07; comparing with R-R: z = −0.49, p=0.63; comparing with R-O: z = 1.16, p=0.25; Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.017; Figure 2I, left panel).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of spatial correlations in object sessions.

claim: RSC border cells encode information that is specific to boundaries of the spatial layout where cell responses differentiate between the types of added features.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that RSC border cells encode information that is specific to boundaries of the spatial layout where cell responses differentiate between the types of added features.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the combined results from wall and object experiments.

claim: There were no significant changes in EMD dissimilarity scores across dim-light and darkness sessions (Boundary EMD score: R1, 0.183 ± 0.001, D1, 0.185 ± 0.003, D2, 0.177 ± 0.003, R2, 0.182 ± 0.002; Friedman test: X2(3)=1.23, p=0.75; n = 21 border cells).
source: We recorded the activity of RSC border cells in both dim-light and darkness conditions, but observed no significant changes in EMD dissimilarity scores across the sessions (Boundary EMD score: R1, 0.183 ± 0.001, D1, 0.185 ± 0.003, D2, 0.177 ± 0.003, R2, 0.182 ± 0.002; Friedman test: X2(3)=1.23, p=0.75; n = 21 border cells; Figure 3B,D).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of border cell activity in darkness.

claim: There were no changes in spatial correlations between different session types in light versus dark conditions (Reg-Reg: r = 0.42 ± 0.03, Reg-Dark: r = 0.38 ± 0.03; Wilcoxon signed-rank test z = 0.61, p=0.54; Dark-Dark: r = 0.42 ± 0.05).
source: There were also no changes across spatial correlations between different session types (Reg-Reg: r = 0.42 ± 0.03, Reg-Dark: r = 0.38 ± 0.03; Wilcoxon signed-rank test z = 0.61, p=0.54; Dark-Dark: r = 0.42 ± 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Reg-Reg correlation, z = 1.20, p=0.23; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.025; Figure 3C), indicating that activity is not generated through visual sensory input.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of spatial correlations in darkness.

claim: Border cell activity is not generated through visual sensory input.
source: There were also no changes across spatial correlations between different session types (Reg-Reg: r = 0.42 ± 0.03, Reg-Dark: r = 0.38 ± 0.03; Wilcoxon signed-rank test z = 0.61, p=0.54; Dark-Dark: r = 0.42 ± 0.05, Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Reg-Reg correlation, z = 1.20, p=0.23; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.025; Figure 3C), indicating that activity is not generated through visual sensory input.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the darkness experiment results.

claim: The majority of border cells were unaffected by wall removal in the drop-edge experiment, with no significant changes in EMD scores (Unaffected cells: boundary EMD score: R1, 0.183 ± 0.002, Drop, 0.186 ± 0.003, R2, 0.183 ± 0.001; Friedman test: X2(2)=4.59, p=0.10; n = 17 border cells).
source: The EMD scores showed that the majority of border cells were unaffected by the wall removal, with no significant changes in the drop-edge session (Unaffected cells: boundary EMD score: R1, 0.183 ± 0.002, Drop, 0.186 ± 0.003, R2, 0.183 ± 0.001; Friedman test: X2(2)=4.59, p=0.10; n = 17 border cells; Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of border cells in the drop-edge experiment.

claim: A subset of cells (n = 8/25) had disrupted firing nearby the boundary edges in the drop-edge experiment.
source: However, a subset of cells had disrupted firing nearby the boundary edges (n = 8/25 affected cells, separated based on an increase in EMD that exceeded the 95th-percentile of a null distribution of change, computed using the differences between first and last regular sessions; boundary EMD score: R1, 0.169 ± 0.008, Drop, 0.202 ± 0.004, R2, 0.175 ± 0.006; Friedman test: X2(2)=11.0, p=0.004; Post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank test: R1-Drop, z = −2.95, p=0.003, R1-R2, z = 0, p=1.0; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.025; Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript reports data on a subset of affected cells in the drop-edge experiment.

claim: Rate map correlations remained high for unaffected cells when comparing regular and drop-edge sessions (Unaffected cells: Reg-Reg, r = 0.50 ± 0.04, Reg-Drop, r = 0.45 ± 0.04; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 1.21, p=0.23).
source: A similar result emerged from the spatial correlations, where rate map correlations remained high when comparing regular and drop-edge sessions, but only for the unaffected cells that had stable EMD scores across session type (Unaffected cells: Reg-Reg, r = 0.50 ± 0.04, Reg-Drop, r = 0.45 ± 0.04; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 1.21, p=0.23; Affected cells: Reg-Reg, r = 0.57 ± 0.05, Reg-Drop, r = 0.14 ± 0.07; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.008; Figure 3H).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of spatial correlations in the drop-edge experiment.

claim: Affected cells showed significantly decreased correlations in the drop-edge session (Affected cells: Reg-Reg, r = 0.57 ± 0.05, Reg-Drop, r = 0.14 ± 0.07; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.008).
source: A similar result emerged from the spatial correlations, where rate map correlations remained high when comparing regular and drop-edge sessions, but only for the unaffected cells that had stable EMD scores across session type (Unaffected cells: Reg-Reg, r = 0.50 ± 0.04, Reg-Drop, r = 0.45 ± 0.04; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 1.21, p=0.23; Affected cells: Reg-Reg, r = 0.57 ± 0.05, Reg-Drop, r = 0.14 ± 0.07; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: p=0.008; Figure 3H).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing disruption in affected cells.

claim: Whisker trimming did not result in a significant change in the proportion of border cells in RSC (intact whiskers: 29/276 cells classified as border cells; trimmed whiskers: 23/285 cells classified as border cells; change in proportion: z = 1.00, p=0.32, binomial test).
source: To directly test the necessity of whisker-mediated tactile sensation, we trimmed the animal's whiskers after which they freely explored the arena (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B). We did not observe a significant change in the proportion of border cells in RSC after the trimming of whiskers (intact whiskers: 29/276 cells classified as border cells, boundary EMD score = 0.183 ± 0.002; trimmed whiskers: 23/285 cells classified as border cells, boundary EMD score = 0.186 ± 0.005; change in proportion of border cells: z = 1.00, p=0.32, binomial test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), nor did we see a change in the overall firing rates (before: FR = 1.58 ± 0.38; after: FR = 1.16 ± 0.47; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 1.04, p=0.30; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that whisker sensation is not essential for boundary representation.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of border cells after whisker trimming.

claim: Whisker trimming did not result in a change in overall firing rates (before: FR = 1.58 ± 0.38; after: FR = 1.16 ± 0.47; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 1.04, p=0.30).
source: To directly test the necessity of whisker-mediated tactile sensation, we trimmed the animal's whiskers after which they freely explored the arena (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B). We did not observe a significant change in the proportion of border cells in RSC after the trimming of whiskers (intact whiskers: 29/276 cells classified as border cells, boundary EMD score = 0.183 ± 0.002; trimmed whiskers: 23/285 cells classified as border cells, boundary EMD score = 0.186 ± 0.005; change in proportion of border cells: z = 1.00, p=0.32, binomial test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), nor did we see a change in the overall firing rates (before: FR = 1.58 ± 0.38; after: FR = 1.16 ± 0.47; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 1.04, p=0.30; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that whisker sensation is not essential for boundary representation.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of firing rates after whisker trimming.

claim: Whisker sensation is not essential for boundary representation.
source: To directly test the necessity of whisker-mediated tactile sensation, we trimmed the animal's whiskers after which they freely explored the arena (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B). We did not observe a significant change in the proportion of border cells in RSC after the trimming of whiskers (intact whiskers: 29/276 cells classified as border cells, boundary EMD score = 0.183 ± 0.002; trimmed whiskers: 23/285 cells classified as border cells, boundary EMD score = 0.186 ± 0.005; change in proportion of border cells: z = 1.00, p=0.32, binomial test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), nor did we see a change in the overall firing rates (before: FR = 1.58 ± 0.38; after: FR = 1.16 ± 0.47; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: z = 1.04, p=0.30; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that whisker sensation is not essential for boundary representation.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the whisker trimming results.

claim: A subpopulation of cells in the barrel field region of the somatosensory cortex (S1bf) fired nearby boundaries (n = 23/173 cells classified as border cells).
source: We further recorded from cells located in the barrel field region of the somatosensory cortex (S1bf) in order to understand the nature of somatosensory information through whiskers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F). Although we were able to identify a subpopulation of cells that fired nearby boundaries in the somatosensory cortex (n = 23/173 cells classified as border cells using the same criteria; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), an important difference with RSC cells is that S1bf neurons fired consistently near added objects when introduced into the arena, highlighting the selective tuning of RSC border cells to boundaries but not objects (Normalized boundary EMD score: R1, 1.0 ± 0, O1, 1.067 ± 0.01, O2, 1.084 ± 0.01, R2, 0.971 ± 0.01; Friedman test: X2(3)=47.1, p=3.3 × 10−10; Post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank test: R1-O1, z = −3.65, p=2.6 × 10−4, R1-O2, z = −3.89, p=9.9 × 10−5, R1-R2, z = 2.95, p=0.003; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.017; Normalized object EMD score: R1, 1.0 ± 0 O1, 0.977 ± 0.005, O2, 0.967 ± 0.005, R2, 1.015 ± 0.004; Friedman test: X2(3)=47.5, p=2.7 × 10−10; Post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank test: R1-O1, z = 3.50, p=4.7 × 10−4, R1-O2, z = 3.80, p=1.4 × 10−4, R1-R2, z = −3.16, p=0.002; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.017; Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The manuscript reports data from S1bf recordings.

claim: S1bf neurons fired consistently near added objects when introduced into the arena, unlike RSC border cells.
source: We further recorded from cells located in the barrel field region of the somatosensory cortex (S1bf) in order to understand the nature of somatosensory information through whiskers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F). Although we were able to identify a subpopulation of cells that fired nearby boundaries in the somatosensory cortex (n = 23/173 cells classified as border cells using the same criteria; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), an important difference with RSC cells is that S1bf neurons fired consistently near added objects when introduced into the arena, highlighting the selective tuning of RSC border cells to boundaries but not objects (Normalized boundary EMD score: R1, 1.0 ± 0, O1, 1.067 ± 0.01, O2, 1.084 ± 0.01, R2, 0.971 ± 0.01; Friedman test: X2(3)=47.1, p=3.3 × 10−10; Post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank test: R1-O1, z = −3.65, p=2.6 × 10−4, R1-O2, z = −3.89, p=9.9 × 10−5, R1-R2, z = 2.95, p=0.003; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.017; Normalized object EMD score: R1, 1.0 ± 0 O1, 0.977 ± 0.005, O2, 0.967 ± 0.005, R2, 1.015 ± 0.004; Friedman test: X2(3)=47.5, p=2.7 × 10−10; Post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank test: R1-O1, z = 3.50, p=4.7 × 10−4, R1-O2, z = 3.80, p=1.4 × 10−4, R1-R2, z = −3.16, p=0.002; Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.017; Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis comparing S1bf and RSC responses to objects.

evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the combined sensory manipulation results.

claim: The RSC has direct, bi-directional connections with the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC).
source: The RSC is known to have direct, bi-directional connections with the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) (Jones and Witter, 2007; Ohara et al., 2018), which contains several types of neurons that exhibit allocentric spatial tuning such as grid cells, head-direction cells or border cells (Boccara et al., 2010; Hafting et al., 2005; Sargolini et al., 2006; Solstad et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous anatomical studies.

claim: Recording of RSC neurons in the absence of inhibitory opsin expression showed stable firing patterns for border cells near all boundaries of the environment before, during and after the application of laser light, with no changes in EMD scores (Boundary EMD score: laser OFF1, 0.173 ± 0.002, laser ON1, 0.176 ± 0.003, laser ON2, 0.174 ± 0.004, laser OFF2, 0.170 ± 0.001; Friedman test: X2(3)=5.44, p=0.14; n = 33 border cells).
